title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
event_hint: CodeGrep: 14B retrieval agent trained with GRPO to reduce coding agent file exploration overhead
problem: Modern LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified, a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, with a large fraction consumed by grep, glob, and view_file calls during ambiguous exploration loops—often 20+ rounds in wrong directions before the agent gives up.
mechanism: CodeGrep is a 14B-parameter retrieval agent built on Qwen3-14B-Instruct, trained end-to-end with GRPO to issue multi-turn parallel grep/glob/read tool calls and return candidate files to a frozen downstream coding agent. It exposes three read-only primitives (regex search, path matching, file contents) mirroring developer navigation. At each turn it emits up to 8 tool calls executed concurrently. During inference, CodeGrep takes the issue description, emits candidate files, and those files are injected into the prompt of a frozen OpenHands downstream agent—only the retriever is trained. Training uses a worktree-based sandbox that replaces Docker images with git worktree add, reducing environment interaction per rollout from minutes to milliseconds. CATM mines 32K samples from 67K open-source agent trajectories (47.7% retention) using GLM-5.1-FP8 as judge model.

evaluation_context: Evaluation on SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances) using OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 as downstream agent, temperature 0, 100-round max. Baseline without retrieval resolves 25.8% at 23.0 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue. Training uses 67K open-source agent trajectories mined via CATM, with GLM-5.1-FP8 as judge model. Training on single 8xB200 node with LoRA, 27-hour wall-clock per run, early-stop at step 897 of 2000-step budget. Environment uses git worktree-based sandbox replacing Docker, enabling per-rollout setup in milliseconds versus minutes. Three-layer architecture extracts unique (repo,commit) pairs, uses git clone --bare and git worktree add for shared object database, and executes grep/glob/read through native subprocesses with 64-way concurrency limit.
limitations: Evaluation limited to SWE-Bench Verified benchmark only—no production deployment data or real-world coding workflows reported. The line-range component was removed because downstream OpenHands editor has no view_range argument, making predicted line ranges dead information at inference time. Training data includes CATM-only entries with no gold line ranges by construction, introducing systematic label bias. The downstream agent is frozen (OpenHands), so results may not generalize to other coding agents like Claude Code. Precision threshold regime characterization based on only three retrievers (BM25, Jina, CodeGrep). End-to-end wall-clock latency not reported, only token and round metrics. Token cost breakdown per tool type (grep vs glob vs read) not reported. Repository index construction cost not explicitly quantified—worktree-based approach described but no specific build time or storage overhead provided. Applying efficiency signal at advantage layer reduces KL drift compared to reward-layer application, but KL still climbs to ~0.02 under v1/v2 before v3 masks only when ¯c>0.
project_relevance: Directly relevant to Agent semantic acceleration focus on reducing repetitive Read, Grep, Glob, and code exploration. CodeGrep demonstrates a clear precision threshold (≈0.45-0.50) below which retrieval degrades downstream agent and above which it buys efficiency. This directly addresses current questions about whether repository indices truly reduce end-to-end task latency—CodeGrep shows 15% rounds reduction and 19% tokens reduction while preserving resolve rate. The work quantifies tool call overhead (2.3 average turns per rollout) and shows retrieval must cross precision ≈0.677 to translate into downstream efficiency. Worktree-based sandbox reduces environment interaction from minutes to milliseconds, enabling single-node training at scale. However, CodeGrep does not address repository index construction cost, false positive rates, error recovery overhead, token cost per-tool breakdown, or whether parallel tool calls introduce correctness risk—limitations that project context specifically asks for.

evidence_gaps.question: What is the token cost breakdown per tool type (grep vs glob vs read) for both CodeGrep and the baseline agent?
What is the overhead comparison between retrieval injection and direct agent exploration in terms of end-to-end wall-clock latency?
What are the repository index construction cost, false positive rate, and error recovery overhead for CodeGrep?
